title: NASA's New Telescope Will See What Even JWST Can't
summary:
The James Webb Space Telescope is famous for taking jaw-dropping pictures of space. But there's a whole part of the universe it literally cannot see. NASA wants to fix that.

A new telescope called PRIMA (Probe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics) is moving forward in its design. If everything goes well, it will launch no earlier than 2033 and run for five years. Its mirror is 5.9 feet (1.8 meters) wide — smaller than JWST's, but it's built to catch a different kind of light: far-infrared.

Think of light like radio stations. JWST listens to near- and mid-infrared channels. PRIMA tunes into far-infrared, which is like a station JWST's radio can't pick up. That matters because certain signals — the kind that tell us where water and carbon are in planet-forming disks — only show up there.

"We can't actually address these science questions with JWST," said Meredith MacGregor, an astronomer at Johns Hopkins University, "because the spectral lines that are required are only in the far-infrared."

PRIMA will study how planets form, how galaxies grow, and how black holes evolve. It costs about $1.2 billion — way less than JWST's $10 billion. One scientist said he's most excited about "the things I don't yet know." Same here.
why_it_matters: It shows how scientists pick the question first — like 'where does the water in planets come from?' — and then build exactly the right machine to answer it, just like choosing the right tool for a school project.

background_read: The James Webb Space Telescope (the huge space telescope NASA launched in 2021) looks at near- and mid-infrared light, and it took many years and about $10 billion to build.
Johns Hopkins University is a big research university in Baltimore, Maryland, in the United States, where Meredith MacGregor works and teaches.
Not all light is the kind our eyes can see: infrared light is the kind that feels like warmth from a heater, and far-infrared is the part with the longest waves of all.
Article_Structure: WHO: NASA, plus astronomer Meredith MacGregor of Johns Hopkins University, who explained why JWST cannot do this job.
WHAT: A new space telescope called PRIMA (Probe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics) has moved forward in its design.
WHERE: It is being designed in the United States and would launch into space, where it would run for five years.
WHY: Far-infrared light carries clues about water and carbon in planet-forming disks, so PRIMA could show how planets form.

perspectives.description: They say PRIMA fills a gap JWST cannot reach, and that its far-infrared channels could finally explain how planets, galaxies, and black holes grow.
Some people argue that a $1.2 billion space telescope is a lot to spend when there are problems to solve here on Earth.
They point out it is still only a design, and big telescopes often take longer and cost more than first planned before they actually launch.
